content.text: A chat turn doesn't cost the tokens of the new message. Every request resends and bills the system prompt, the tool definitions and the whole history, so each turn costs more than the last and a long session costs many times what a per-message estimate predicts. Measure it with the
usage
fields, then cut the repeated part with prompt caching.

A team launches an internal assistant and budgets it from the average message: about 200 tokens in and 400 out. The first invoice is several times the budget. The questions weren't longer than expected; the sessions were. By the thirtieth turn of a conversation, every request carried the system prompt, the tool definitions and twenty-nine earlier exchanges, and each of those tokens was billed again.
The common misconception
"Each chat turn only costs the tokens of the new message I send." It's a natural assumption:

items.text: A chat UI shows one new message per turn, so that feels like the unit of work.
Pricing pages list a price per million tokens, which invites "message size × price".
The first turns of a session are cheap, so early tests confirm the estimate.
Chat products and SDK helpers manage history for you, and message threads (in beta) even let a request send only the new messages.

content.text: The half-truth: you do pay per token, and the new message is part of what you pay for. But the tokens you pay for on a turn are everything the model reads on that turn, and that's far more than what you typed.
What actually happens
Every turn re-reads the conversation

As the Understanding LLMs path showed, the Messages API is stateless: you send the full conversational history on every request. Message threads don't change the bill either; Anthropic's docs say they make requests smaller and faster to start, but threads "do not change pricing". The model reads the whole
context
again, and you pay for reading it.
What's in each request's bill
On Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic's pricing page lists $4 per million input
tokens
and $20 per million output tokens. Input on a given turn includes:

items.text: Tool definitions, plus a tool-use system prompt the API adds when you send
(286 tokens on Claude Opus 5.5 with automatic tool choice).
Every earlier user and assistant message, including tool results, which are often the bulkiest part.

Earlier thinking. Thinking is billed as output when it's generated, even when its text isn't returned to you, and on models that keep prior thinking in context, such as recent Opus models, it's billed as input on later turns too.

content.text: Output is the reply plus that turn's thinking, at five times the input price.
The arithmetic: linear per turn, quadratic per session
Because each request carries all earlier turns, the input of turn
n
grows in a straight line with
n

. Summed over a session, that's a quadratic curve. Take a chat with a 3,000-token system prompt and tools, 200-token questions and 400-token answers on Claude Opus 5.5. Turn 1 sends 3,200 tokens; turn 10 sends 8,600; turn 30 sends 20,600. A per-message estimate for 30 turns says $0.26. The model below says $1.67.

blocks.code:
PRICE = {"in": 4.00, "write": 5.00, "read": 0.20, "out": 20.00}  # $/MTok


def chat_cost(turns, system=3_000, ask=200, answer=400, cached=False):
    cost, cached_prefix = 0.0, 0
    for turn in range(1, turns + 1):
        sent = system + turn * ask + (turn - 1) * answer  # full history
        if cached:  # earlier turns are cache reads, the new tail a write
            cost += cached_prefix * PRICE["read"]
            cost += (sent - cached_prefix) * PRICE["write"]
            cached_prefix = sent
        else:
            cost += sent * PRICE["in"]
        cost += answer * PRICE["out"]
    return cost / 1_000_000


print(f"uncached ${chat_cost(30):.2f}")  # uncached $1.67
print(f"cached ${chat_cost(30, cached=True):.2f}")  # cached $0.41

content.text: Caching changes the price of the repeat, not its size
Prompt caching
stores the processed prefix of a request (
tools
, then
system
, then
messages
) and reuses it when a later request starts with exactly the same content. With automatic caching, one top-level
cache_control
field moves the cache point to the end of each request as the chat grows, so every turn reads the earlier conversation from the cache and writes only the new part.

On Claude Opus 5.5, a cache read costs 0.05 times the base input price ($0.20 per million) and a 5-minute cache write costs 1.25 times ($5). That's the cached line in the model: $0.41 instead of $1.67. Notice what's left: $0.24 of it is output, which caching never touches.

The docs list the conditions. The default cache lives 5 minutes and every hit refreshes it at no extra cost; a 1-hour cache costs 2 times the base price to write. Prompts shorter than the model's minimum, 512 tokens on Claude Opus 5.5, aren't cached and no error is returned. And any change to the prefix invalidates what follows it: edit a tool definition and the whole cache is gone.
Read the real numbers from
usage
Every response reports what you were billed for. With caching on,
input_tokens
counts only the tokens after the last cache breakpoint. Total input is
cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens
. A meter that estimates from the new message misses almost all of it.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
def ask(text):
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": text})
    reply = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000,
        system=SYSTEM, messages=history,
    )
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply.content})
    new_tokens = len(text) // 4  # only the new message: the bill disagrees
    meter.add_usd((new_tokens * 4.00 + reply.usage.output_tokens * 20.00) / 1e6)
    return reply


ask("Why does the CSV export fail with E413?")

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
def ask(text):
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": text})
    reply = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, system=SYSTEM,
        messages=history, cache_control={"type": "ephemeral"},
    )
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply.content})
    u = reply.usage  # all input = input + cache writes + cache reads
    meter.add_usd((u.input_tokens * 4.00
                   + (u.cache_creation_input_tokens or 0) * 5.00
                   + (u.cache_read_input_tokens or 0) * 0.20
                   + u.output_tokens * 20.00) / 1e6)
    return reply


ask("Why does the CSV export fail with E413?")

rows.text: A turn costs the new message plus the reply
It costs everything sent: system prompt, tools, all history, plus the reply
Cost grows with the number of messages
Per-turn input grows linearly, so session cost grows quadratically
It's billed as output, and on keep-all models as input on later turns
Message threads mean you stop paying for history
Threads make requests smaller; they don't change pricing
It makes repeated input cheaper; the model still reads all of it

content.text: The token counting endpoint,
client.messages.count_tokens()

, takes the same inputs as a message request and is free to use, within its own rate limits. Use it to check a long request against a budget before sending it. The count is an estimate, and models from Claude 4.7 on use a tokenizer that produces about 30 percent more tokens for the same text, so recount when you change models.

blocks.title: One timestamp can switch caching off

content.text: The cache matches the prefix exactly. A current time, a request ID or a reordered tool list near the top of the prompt changes the prefix on every call, so nothing is ever read from the cache and no error tells you. If
cache_read_input_tokens
stays at 0 across turns, look for the part of the prefix that changes.
How to apply it in your project
Record all four
usage
fields with the conversation ID and turn number. Chart cost by turn, not just per day, and the long sessions show up.

items.title: Turn on caching and keep the prefix stable

content.text: Add a top-level
cache_control
, put fixed content first and volatile content last, and check
cache_read_input_tokens
in your logs.
Trim tool results to the fields the model needs and summarize or drop old turns. The Building with LLMs path returns to this in its context engineering article.
Set a token or dollar ceiling per conversation and decide what happens when it's reached: summarize, start fresh or hand off.
For jobs nobody waits on, the Batch API halves the price: $2 input and $10 output per million tokens on Claude Opus 5.5.
Key takeaways

items.text: Every request bills the full context again: system prompt, tool definitions, all earlier turns and their tool results.
Per-turn cost grows linearly, so a long session costs far more than a per-message estimate.
Thinking is billed as output, and on recent models earlier thinking is billed again as input.
Prompt caching makes the repeated prefix much cheaper, but it can't reduce output or what the model has to read.
fields and count tokens before sending, then optimize what the numbers show.
